extracted.intended_audience: learned readers and natural philosophers interested in method, natural philosophy, anatomy, and medicine
extracted.subtask_description: A methodological exposition for natural philosophy: how to choose first principles, combine deduction and experiment, study anatomy and physiology, and communicate findings for practical application (especially medicine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept only propositions as certain as geometric demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Resolve to accept as true nothing that does not appear more clear and certain than the demonstrations of the geometers had formerly appeared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational epistemic rule the author adopts (applied to demonstrations of God and the soul). It functions as a methodological constraint to avoid assent to dubious opinions and to produce results with the highest degree of certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive laws of nature from simple, natural notions (first principles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the principles or first causes of all that is or can be in the world from certain germs of truths naturally existing in our minds and from consideration of God's infinite perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use minimal, universally intelligible principles so that derived laws would hold in any possible world created under the same laws. The author claims many phenomena (heavens, stars, earth, elements) can be deduced from such principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use imaginative hypothesis of a newly created world as a methodological device
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid being bound to learned disputes, suppose a new world created with matter agitated into chaos and then acting only under God’s established laws, and reason what would naturally result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This thought-experiment approach simplifies assumptions (no prior scholastic forms) and lets one deduce how matter would arrange itself, helping to infer general laws and typical outcomes (formation of heavens, planets, earth, tides, currents, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus exposition on a principal subject, casting others into shade
rubrics_metrics.description: Select one chief object (as a painter selects one face of a solid) on which to make the light fall and treat it at length, allowing other topics to appear only as they relate to the principal one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice for writing and investigation: concentrate effort on one central phenomenon (the author chose light) and then add related topics (sun, stars, heavens, planets, earth, living beings) in relation to it to avoid overextension and preserve clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground physiological claims in direct anatomical observation and dissection
rubrics_metrics.description: Advise those not versed in anatomy to have a large animal heart dissected before them to observe ventricles, major vessels, valves (pellicles), auricles, and textures to understand heart motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical, demonstrative instruction: recommend hands-on observation of organs to follow subsequent mechanistic explanations of motion and function; details about specific structures (vena cava, arterial vein, venous artery, valves) are provided as observational anchors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain bodily functions by mechanical and thermal mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the motion of the heart, pulse, heating of blood, rarefaction and dilation by heat, valve action, and arterial/venous dynamics by appeal to arrangement of parts and heat (analogy to clockwork).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physiological explanation should follow necessarily from observable arrangement of parts, touchable warmth, and known properties of blood; the author repeatedly invokes mechanical/thermal causation rather than occult qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize ordinary, common phenomena in experimentation before rare ones
rubrics_metrics.description: At the commencement, it is better to make use only of what is spontaneously presented to our senses and worth slight reflection, than to concern ourselves about more uncommon and recondite phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: uncommon phenomena often mislead while causes of ordinary phenomena remain unknown; ordinary cases are easier to know and provide firmer grounds for further investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase reliance on particular experiments as knowledge advances
rubrics_metrics.description: When descending to more particular questions, appeal to many particular experiments to distinguish forms or species and to discover how diverse objects are generated or applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A staged method: start from first causes and common effects, then use systematic experiments to resolve more special or minute circumstances that cannot be inferred by pure reflection alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish and communicate findings to enable collective, cumulative progress
rubrics_metrics.description: Faithfully communicate to the public all discoveries to incite others of superior genius to make further experiments so that connecting many lives and labours we may collectively proceed farther than individuals alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication is advocated as an effective provision against the shortness of life and experiment scarcity: sharing results enables others to continue, replicate, and extend the work for practical benefits (arts, medicine).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for practical application (arts and medicine) from natural philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer a practical philosophy that, knowing the force and action of fire, water, air, stars, and other bodies as crafts are known, allows us to apply them to many uses and to be lords and possessors of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit instrumental goal: discoveries should lead to inventions and particularly to advances in medicine (preservation of health). The author judges present medical knowledge inadequate and sees promise in applying physical laws to remedies and cures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh risks of publication relative to social and religious censure
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about publishing doctrines if they may be condemned by authorities or judged prejudicial to religion or the state; such censure may justify withholding publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While advocating openness, the author acknowledges prudential reasons (fear of causing hurt, social/religious consequences) that may alter the decision to publish; this shapes when and how to disseminate findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish rational minds from machines by adaptive use of language and general reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: A true rational soul cannot be produced from matter alone; machines, however well constructed, could not use words or signs flexibly to declare thoughts, nor act from universal reason rather than fixed organ dispositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two empirical tests are proposed: (1) capacity to combine words/signs to declare thoughts appropriately in varied contexts; (2) ability to act from general reason rather than from a particular organ arrangement (machines need particular organs per action). Examples: parrots and magpies utter words without understanding; deaf-mutes invent signs that show reasoning capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer the necessity of a created rational soul from differences between humans and brutes
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasonable soul must be expressly created and more closely united to the body than a mere pilot-in-a-ship relation to account for sensations, appetites, and true human capacities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion is used for metaphysical claims about immortality: because brutes lack language-derived reasoning and certain human faculties, the human rational soul cannot be explained by matter alone and is therefore of a different, possibly immortal nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infer circulation via small passages between arteries and veins (capillary reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be many small passages at the extremities of the arteries through which blood received from the heart passes into small branches of the veins, whence it returns to the heart—a perpetual circulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument rests on surgical experience (effects of ligature), observation of venous valves, rapid loss of blood from a single cut artery even when tied near the heart, and structural differences between arterial and venous coats; used as a methodological example of combining experiment, observation, and mechanical reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple lines of empirical evidence to corroborate physiological explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Support claims about heart, pulse, blood heating, respiration, digestion, and nutrition by diverse observations: differences in arterial vs venous blood, vessel textures, pulse sensation, effects of respiration (lungs converting rarefied blood), and digestive heat distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological injunction: do not rely on single observations; instead combine anatomical texture, pulse palpation, ligature experiments, comparative anatomy (animals without lungs), and functional consequences (digestion, nutrition, generation of animal spirits) to form a coherent explanatory account.
